title: Speciation and the Tree of Life

cards.b: Life on Earth has millions of species, yet all come from one common ancestor. Understanding how species split and how we group them gives a map of life, and helps in conservation and medicine.

Ernst Mayr's biological species concept (1942): a group of populations that interbreed in nature and are reproductively isolated from others. It is not perfect: it fails for asexual organisms and fossils, where shape or genes are used.

1. A population is split (a river, mountain or sea).
  2. Each side faces different conditions and drifts apart genetically.
  3. Eventually they can no longer interbreed.

• Before mating: different habitat, timing, courtship or body shape.
  • After mating: hybrids are weak or sterile. The mule (horse x donkey) is sterile.

Sympatric speciation, with no barrier, happens in plants through chromosome doubling (polyploidy), and in some fish by habitat choice.

When a lineage enters many open habitats it splits quickly into many forms. Darwin's finches in the Galapagos and the cichlid fishes of African lakes are classic cases. After the dinosaur extinction about 66 million years ago, mammals radiated.

Carolus Linnaeus (1735) gave binomial names such as Homo sapiens. Today, we use phylogenetic trees that show descent, built from DNA. Carl Woese (1977) found three domains: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya. Classic ranks: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.

More than 99 percent of species that ever lived are extinct. Five mass extinctions are known; the end-Permian (about 252 million years ago) killed up to 90 percent of marine species. Many scientists say we are in a sixth, driven by humans.

Hawaiian fruit flies and island lizards show species forming. Ring species such as the Ensatina salamanders in California show neighbours can breed while the ends cannot. DNA clocks estimate when lineages split.

Fix these

  • A tree of life is not a ladder; humans are not the 'top'.
  • Species do not 'try' to split.
  • Modern animals are not ancestors of each other; they are cousins.

India holds about 8 percent of the world's recorded species on 2.4 percent of land. It has four biodiversity hotspots: the Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, and Sundaland (Nicobar). Island species, such as those on the Andaman and Nicobar islands, show allopatric speciation. The Zoological Survey of India (1916) and Botanical Survey of India (1890) document them.

• Species: reproductively isolated groups.
  • Isolation plus divergence leads to speciation.
  • Three domains: Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya.
  • Extinction is normal but is now accelerating.

Think about it:

  1. Why do islands have so many unique species?
  2. Why is a mule sterile although it is healthy?
